Chapter 3 of 5 // Music & Contract Lore

Stadium Anthems & The 1986 Redline

"Ignition" (1986) //, The Stomp (1989) //, "Saturday Night Lights" (Oct 8, 2004)

1. The Birth of "Ignition (The Forger's Call)"

How a raw garage-metal cassette tape became the most terrifying pre-game entrance ritual in college football.

In October 1986, the O'Connell siblings and Wright twins (soon to be The Stardust Engine) entered a student-run contest to replace the traditional marching band fanfare that the CPI football team ran onto the field to. In their two-car garage on Progress Street NE, they recorded "Ignition (The Forger's Call)"—a heavy, pounding industrial-rock track anchored by drummer Tyler Wright striking a salvaged automobile brake drum with a sledgehammer (TING... BOOM!). On Saturday, October 18, 1986, the raw garage cassette made its thunderous pre-game debut over the PA system inside The Crucible—launching a Saturday night tradition that has shaken the Blacksburg valley ever since.

The 1986 Progress Street Redline: How a Dual-Enrolled 16-Year-Old Outsmarted University Counsel

When the CPI Student Government Association handed out the entry packet for the October 1986 anthem contest, the back of the standard release form contained a buried "Work Made for Hire" clause that would have transferred 100% of the winning song's master and publishing rights to the CPI Athletic Foundation. Sixteen-year-old prodigy Holly O'Connell—who was dual-enrolled at Blacksburg High School and CPI, riding Blue Ridge Transit Route 1 to campus every afternoon to take undergraduate business and contract law electives—refused to let her siblings and cousins sign it.

Sitting at the Progress Street kitchen table with a red pen days before the October 18, 1986 stadium debut, Holly struck the Work-for-Hire clause and negotiated a $1.00 Perpetual Mutual Cross-License with CPI's Office of University Counsel. Under Holly's agreement, The Stardust Engine retained 100% of their master and publishing rights while granting CPI Athletics and the Marching Forgers a perpetual, royalty-free synchronization license to blast "Ignition" (and future Stardust Engine anthems) inside The Crucible. In exchange, CPI's Office of Trademarks & Licensing granted the band (and any label they wholly owned) a perpetual, worldwide, royalty-free Co-Existence & Artistic Reference License to sing and print CPI, Commonwealth Polytechnic Institute, The Forgers, and The Crucible in their songs and liner notes. Eighteen years later, in October 2004, Holly pulled that exact 1986 contract from the Engine Room Records vault to stage the most famous secret song premiere in college football history—and on October 18, 2011, the band celebrated the exact 25th Anniversary of "Ignition" debuting inside The Crucible by releasing their Burnout Hiatus retrospective, Starfield Calibration.

The 1989 Rivalry Game (Virginia Piedmont University) & "The Stomp"

What makes the tradition legendary is that its most terrifying element didn't exist when the band submitted their raw cassette in 1986. The rhythmic "Stomp" and the deafening crowd chants of "IGNITION!" evolved completely organically during a freezing November 1989 night game against traditional state rivals Virginia Piedmont University (VPU). Trying to stay warm and get rowdy, students packed into the North End Zone (The Anvil) started stomping their heavy winter boots on the galvanized metal bleachers in perfect time with Tyler’s recorded brake drum: TING... BOOM!

Because it was heavy boots on hollow steel bleachers, it echoed across the valley like cannon fire. During the pauses where Ryan screams "IGNITION!" on the tape, visiting VPU fans tried to boo—so 20,000 CPI students spontaneously roared "IGNITION!" right back at the PA system while mimicking the Marching Forgers' bridge cadence (swaying Left, Right, Left, Right in unison). By the mid-1990s, the Athletic Director cemented the ritual by cutting the stadium lights to pitch black right before the tape rolls, leaving opposing teams in the dark listening to 65,000 people register on the campus seismographs.

2. "BAH! BAH! BAH!": The Ironheads & The October 8, 2004 Secret Premiere

OCT 8, 2004 — 4TH QUARTER

How Holly O'Connell ambushed 65,000 fans during the Coal & Iron Border War against #6 Monongahela State—48 hours before Progress Street hit record stores.

Who Are "The Ironheads"?

Just as Buchanan University basketball is famous ph and wide for The Pavilion Lunatics inside Buchanan Indoor Pavilion, Commonwealth Polytechnic Institute football is known across the nation for The Ironheads—the diehard, fanatical student vanguard packed shoulder-to-shoulder onto the cold galvanized metal bleachers of the North End Zone (The Anvil).

Named in dual tribute to CPI's blue-collar metallurgy heritage and legendary benefactor Jeremiah "Ironhead" Vance (Class of '52), The Ironheads wear painted maroon-and-orange steel-mill hard hats and overalls, refuse to sit down from kickoff to the final whistle, and treat acoustic decibel meters on the sidelines as a personal scoreboard.

The Black Anvil Trophy ("The Coal & Iron War") OCT 8, 2004
VISITOR (#6 IN NATION)
MSU Coalminers
13
HOME (THE CRUCIBLE)
CPI Forgers
19

The Stage: The Stardust Engine's homecoming album Progress Street was scheduled for release on Monday, October 10, 2004. Two nights earlier—on Saturday, October 8, 2004—CPI hosted fierce Appalachian border rival #6 Monongahela State University (MSU) inside The Crucible. Behind closed doors, Holly O'Connell had already executed a confidential addendum under her 1986 $1.00 Perpetual Mutual Cross-License with the CPI Athletic Director. Only three people in Blacksburg knew what was on the unmarked gold master CD-R hand-delivered to the press-box audio booth before kickoff.

As the clock hit 0:00 at the end of a bruising third quarter, CPI clung to a gritty fourth-quarter lead over #6 Monongahela State. Normally, the break between the third and fourth quarters belonged to the stadium organ or a standard marching fanfare. Instead, the press-box engineer faded the stadium lights to a deep twilight glow and pushed the master fader all the way up on Track 6 of Progress Street: "Saturday Night Lights: The Crucible."

For the first four bars, 65,000 fans froze as Cassidy's triumphant 1980s analog synthesizer brass fanfare and Tyler's drumline cadence rolled across the valley. Then Ryan and Cassidy's voices echoed from the giant speaker arrays above The Anvil—singing directly about October '86, Progress Street, and "Sixty thousand standing in the maroon and orange sea / Waiting for the signal at CPI with me!"

When The Ironheads realized they were hearing a brand-new, unreleased Stardust Engine stadium anthem written specifically for them, The Crucible detonated. Just as Boston Beacons fans belt the eighth-inning horn hook of "Sweet Evangeline" at Back Bay Park, The Ironheads spontaneously locked onto Cassidy's three-note synthesizer brass fanfare at the end of every chorus line—roaring a deafening, stadium-shaking "BAH! BAH! BAH!" and chanting "SO GOOD! SO GOOD! SO GOOD!" between the verses. Riding the tidal wave of that fourth-quarter singalong, the Forgers defense stuffed Monongahela State's final drive to seal a 19–13 victory. By Monday morning, when Progress Street officially dropped on October 10th, the fourth-quarter "Saturday Night Lights" singalong was already cemented as an unbreakable CPI game-day tradition—turning "Ignition" into the pre-game war cry that starts the fire, and "Saturday Night Lights: The Crucible" into the fourth-quarter victory celebration that seals it.

The Stardust Engine (ERR-001)

Named after the very first song Ryan, Cassidy, Evan, and Tyler wrote together at CPI in 1986—celebrating their shared love of the cosmos (“Stardust”) and the rockets to get you there (“Engine”).
